title: Cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) in performance consulting
body: CBT rests on the cognitive model: it is not a situation by itself but how a person interprets it that shapes emotions, body reactions and behavior. A diver who reads a racing heart as "I'm about to fail" feels and acts differently from one who reads it as "I'm ready." CBT work is structured and collaborative. Sessions often have an agenda, goals are explicit, and clients practice between sessions. The consultant uses guided discovery, asking Socratic questions about the evidence for and against an automatic thought so the client reaches a more balanced view on their own rather than being told it is wrong. Behavioral experiments test beliefs directly: the client makes a prediction, tries the feared action in a planned way (often while dropping a safety behavior), and compares what happened with what they expected. In assessment, the consultant asks what the client was thinking in key moments. Unlicensed CMPCs apply these methods to performance; they don't diagnose or treat disorders.
points: Cognitive model: interpretation → emotion, physiology, behavior
Structured, collaborative, goal-directed, with between-session practice
Cognitive restructuring through guided discovery (Socratic questioning)
Behavioral experiments: predict, test, compare
examNote: Look for agendas, homework, "what went through your mind?" questions and evidence-weighing. Changing thought content is CBT; changing the relationship to thoughts is ACT.

title: Person-centered and humanistic core conditions
body: Carl Rogers proposed that change happens through the relationship. The client, not the consultant, is the expert on their own experience and has a natural tendency toward growth when the conditions are right. Of the conditions he described, three are provided by the helper. Congruence (genuineness) means the consultant's outward behavior matches what they actually feel, with no professional façade. Unconditional positive regard means accepting the person regardless of what they report or achieve; warmth that rises after wins and cools after losses is conditional regard. Accurate empathic understanding means sensing the client's inner world and communicating that understanding back, usually through reflections of feeling and meaning rather than reassurance, advice or fact-finding. In performance work, a person-centered consultant explains the process as client-directed, follows the client's lead when something important comes up mid-session, and treats the relationship itself as the main vehicle of change.
points: Client as expert; actualizing tendency
Congruence, unconditional positive regard, accurate empathy
Empathy is shown through reflections, not reassurance or advice
Nondirective; the relationship drives change
examNote: Expect items asking which response conveys empathy or which condition is missing. Reassurance and advice-giving are common distractors.

title: ACT and the Mindfulness-Acceptance-Commitment (MAC) approach
body: Acceptance and commitment therapy aims for psychological flexibility: being in contact with the present moment and acting on what matters even while unpleasant thoughts and feelings are present. Six interrelated processes support this. Acceptance is willingness to have internal experiences without fighting them. Cognitive defusion means seeing thoughts as passing mental events rather than literal truths, as in "I'm having the thought that I'm too old." Present-moment contact is flexible, nonjudgmental attention to the here and now. Self-as-context is a stable observing perspective that is distinct from any single thought. Values are freely chosen directions, and committed action is behavior guided by them. ACT reads thought suppression and avoidance of situations as experiential avoidance, which tends to maintain the problem. Gardner and Moore's MAC approach applies these ideas to performance. The goal shifts from controlling or eliminating anxiety to noticing it while attending to task-relevant cues and committing to values-driven performance behavior.
points: Six processes: acceptance, defusion, present moment, self-as-context, values, committed action
Target is the relationship to thoughts, not their content
Suppression and avoidance are seen as experiential avoidance
MAC: accept internal states and commit to task-focused, values-driven action
examNote: Distractors are often control strategies (thought stopping, relaxation "until the nerves are gone") or CBT evidence-weighing. Those are inconsistent with ACT and MAC.

title: Solution-focused approach
body: Solution-focused brief therapy, developed by Steve de Shazer, Insoo Kim Berg and colleagues, is future-oriented and strengths-based. It spends little time analyzing where a problem came from. Instead it clarifies what the client wants instead and builds on what already works. Exceptions are times when the problem was absent or smaller, such as the games when a pitcher settled after a walk. The consultant asks what was different then and helps the client do more of it. Scaling questions ("Where are you from 1 to 10?") turn vague goals into steps. Typical follow-ups are what puts the rating where it is rather than lower, and what one point higher would look like in concrete, observable behavior. The miracle question asks the client to imagine the problem resolved overnight and describe what they would notice first, which helps define a preferred future. The client is treated as resourceful, and the consultant uses the client's own language and existing strengths rather than importing new techniques first.
points: Future- and strengths-focused; little time on problem origins
Exception questions: when is the problem absent or smaller?
Scaling questions point to the next small, observable step
Miracle question defines the preferred future
examNote: Problem-history questions ("When did it start?") and searching for negative thoughts are the usual wrong answers when a solution-focused approach is specified.

title: Feminist approaches
body: Feminist approaches start from the view that the personal is political. Individual distress is understood within its sociocultural context, including gender, power and other social structures, rather than located only inside the client. The relationship is egalitarian. The consultant demystifies the process by explaining methods and their rationale, invites the client to question them, shares decisions about goals, and is open about their own values instead of claiming neutrality. In conceptualization, the consultant asks how the environment contributes. Examples include a culture that brushes off a woman's ideas, or unequal access to facilities. This guards against simply accepting a client's self-blame. In delivery, the emphasis is empowerment: validating real inequities and helping clients recognize and use their own power, including collective advocacy through appropriate channels. The consultant does not reframe inequities away, and does not take over without the client's collaboration; advocacy agreed with the client is compatible. These approaches address gender-role socialization for clients of any gender.
points: The personal is political: distress in sociocultural context
Egalitarian relationship; demystify the process; values are not hidden
Empowerment and collaborative advocacy rather than taking over
Examine power and gender rather than defaulting to self-blame
examNote: Correct answers share power and examine context. Wrong answers present the consultant as the expert, claim value-neutrality, pathologize reactions to real inequity, or have the consultant take over without the client's agreement.

title: Systems and ecological approaches
body: Systems theory treats a family, team or organization as a set of interacting parts. A change in one part ripples through the others. Causality is circular rather than linear. A coach yells, defenders tighten up, more shots reach the goalie, the goalie's anxiety rises, and the coach yells more. Each behavior is both cause and effect, so the consultant asks what pattern keeps the problem going rather than who is to blame, and intervenes on the interaction pattern. The person labeled as the problem may be where strain shows most, though individual concerns still need assessment. Bronfenbrenner's ecological model adds nested contexts: the immediate settings of family, school and club; the links between them; settings that affect the athlete indirectly, such as a parent's workplace or a sport federation; and surrounding cultural values. A systems-oriented consultant explains early that key adults or stakeholders may be part of the work, with consent and clear confidentiality limits. Assessment asks how changes at home, school and in sport connect.
points: Teams, families and organizations are interacting systems
Circular, not linear, causality; target the pattern
Ecological view: nested, interacting settings around the athlete
Involving stakeholders requires consent and clear confidentiality limits
examNote: Choose answers that look at interactions across people or settings. Answers that "fix" a single individual, or blame a single cause, reflect linear thinking.

title: Transtheoretical model (stages of change)
body: Prochaska and DiClemente's transtheoretical model describes readiness for change in stages. In precontemplation, the person has no intention to change, often because they see no problem. In contemplation, they intend to change within roughly six months but feel ambivalent. In preparation, they intend to act soon and have taken small steps. In action, they are actively changing. In maintenance, they are sustaining the change and preventing relapse. The practical lesson is to match strategies to the stage. With precontemplators, build rapport and raise awareness without pushing. With contemplators, explore pros and cons (decisional balance) and build confidence. With people in preparation, make concrete plans. In action and maintenance, use behavioral strategies such as cues, scheduling, support and relapse-prevention planning. Mismatching, such as handing a detailed action plan to someone who sees no reason to change, can increase resistance, although research support for strict stage-matching is mixed. Relapse is common and people often recycle through stages. It is normalized, and the consultant re-engages strategies that fit current readiness.
points: Precontemplation → contemplation → preparation → action → maintenance
Match the strategy to the stage
Decisional balance is key early; self-efficacy grows across stages and supports action and maintenance
Relapse is normal; people recycle through stages
examNote: Identify the stage from the client's words, then reject action-stage tactics for early-stage clients and passive waiting for anyone.

title: Theory of planned behavior
body: Ajzen's theory of planned behavior explains deliberate behaviors such as attending training, doing an injury-prevention warm-up, or exercising regularly. Three determinants shape intention, and intention is the most immediate predictor of behavior. The first is attitude toward the behavior: is it good, worthwhile, enjoyable? The second is subjective norms: do important others expect it, and do I care what they think? The third is perceived behavioral control: how easy or possible is it for me, given time, skill and barriers? Perceived control can also predict behavior directly when it reflects real control. For consultants, the model works as a diagnostic map. Assessment asks about all three determinants plus intention. Planning then targets a determinant that is weak and matters for that behavior. If people already value exercise and feel supported but believe they cannot fit it in, a benefits campaign or more endorsements miss the point. Protected time, short sessions and barrier planning address the real problem, which is low perceived control.
points: Attitudes + subjective norms + perceived behavioral control → intention → behavior
Perceived behavioral control can also influence behavior directly
Assess all three determinants and intention
Intervene on a weak determinant that matters for the behavior
examNote: Don't confuse TPB with stages of change (TTM), SDT's basic needs, or the health belief model's susceptibility and severity.

title: Philosophy of practice and models of performance excellence
body: Poczwardowski, Sherman and Ravizza describe a professional philosophy as layered. At the base are core beliefs and values about people and change. On top of these sit a theoretical paradigm, then a model of practice and the consultant's role, then intervention goals, and finally techniques. Two consultants using the same techniques may relate to clients very differently because their deeper beliefs differ. Good practice is consistent: a consultant who values self-reliance takes an educational role and hands responsibility to athletes, and a consultant with a cognitive view plans work on interpretations. A clear philosophy also lets consultants describe their approach honestly so clients can judge fit. Models of excellence inform what consultants build. Orlick and Partington's study of Olympians highlighted commitment, quality practice, mental preparation and focus plans, distraction control and post-competition evaluation. Gould, Dieffenbach and Moffett found that Olympic champions showed characteristics such as anxiety control, confidence, focus, goal setting and optimism, developed over years through parents, coaches and the sport environment.
points: Core beliefs → paradigm → model and role → goals → techniques
Consistency across layers is the mark of a sound philosophy
Orlick and Partington: commitment, quality practice, mental readiness, evaluation
Gould et al.: champion characteristics are developed, not simply innate
examNote: When asked what explains differences between consultants, or which plan fits a stated philosophy, trace back to core beliefs and pick the option consistent across the layers.
